content: Various solutions have been proposed for wound cleansing, but normal saline is often preferred due to its isotonic nature, which is believed not to interfere with the natural healing process. Tap water, on the other hand, is frequently used in community settings because it is readily available, cost-effective, and efficient. However, its use remains a topic of debate. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of water, in its various forms, for wound cleansing. For the most recent update in May 2021, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing or unpublished studies, and reference lists of relevant studies, reviews, and meta-analyses were examined. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, and quasi-RCTs were excluded in this update. Thirteen trials involving 2504 participants aged between 2 and 95 years were included. Participants had various types of wounds, including open fractures, surgical wounds, traumatic wounds, anal fissures, and chronic wounds. The trials were conducted in six countries, with most taking place in India and the USA. The comparisons included cleansing with tap water versus no cleansing, tap water versus normal saline, distilled water versus normal saline, cooled boiled water versus normal saline, and distilled water versus cooled boiled water. Wound Infection: No trials reported on wound infection when comparing tap water with no cleansing. Eight trials comparing tap water with normal saline showed that the effect on wound infection rates is uncertain (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.19), with very low-certainty evidence. Two trials comparing distilled water with normal saline for cleansing open fractures found the effect on infection rates to be uncertain (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.09), with very low-certainty evidence. One trial comparing cooled boiled water with normal saline for cleansing open fractures also found the effect on infection rates to be uncertain (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.87), with very low-certainty evidence. The same trial compared distilled water with cooled boiled water and found the effect on infection rates to be uncertain (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.47), with very low-certainty evidence. Wound Healing: Three trials comparing tap water with no cleansing suggested there may be little or no difference in the number of wounds that failed to heal (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.14), with low-certainty evidence. The effect of tap water compared with normal saline on wound healing is uncertain, based on pooled results from two trials (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.07), with very low-certainty evidence. One study comparing distilled water with normal saline for cleansing open fractures found that all wounds healed, and there may be little or no difference in healing rates, but the certainty of the evidence is low. Reduction in Wound Size: The effect of cleansing with tap water compared with normal saline on wound size reduction is uncertain (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.68), with very low-certainty evidence. Rate of Wound Healing: The effect of cleansing with tap water compared with normal saline on the rate of wound healing is uncertain (MD -3.06, 95% CI -6.70 to 0.58), with very low-certainty evidence. Costs: Two trials reported cost analyses, but the cost-effectiveness of tap water compared with normal saline remains uncertain, with very low-certainty evidence. Pain: One study comparing tap water with no cleansing for acute and chronic wounds found that there may be little or no difference in pain scores, with low-certainty evidence. Patient Satisfaction: One study comparing tap water with no cleansing for acute and chronic wounds found that there may be little or no difference in patient satisfaction, with low-certainty evidence. Conclusions: The evidence from this review is of low or very low certainty. Cleansing wounds with tap water may result in little or no difference in healing compared with no cleansing, and there is no data on its impact on wound infection. The effects of cleansing with tap water, cooled boiled water, or distilled water compared with normal saline are uncertain. Similarly, the comparison between distilled water and cooled boiled water is inconclusive. Data on other outcomes are limited and either uncertain or suggest minimal differences in results.
